deep.reconstruction:
The page shows a single worked example: an arrangement of seven pseudo-lines, labelled A–G, drawn in a disk. This is the usual affine or disk model of an arrangement in the projective plane. Each pseudo-line meets the boundary circle twice. On the left and top the ends read A, B, C, D, E, F, G; on the right and bottom they read in reversed order, the antipodal identification. Near the top and the bottom of the disk are two marked poles.

Thin pencil curves run between the two poles. They look like a sweeping family, a 'pencil' of pseudo-lines through two points that sweeps the disk from left to right. The crossing points of the arrangement are labelled 1 to 19. These labels act as levels or times in the sweep, and several crossings share a level (two 18s, two 19s, repeated 4s and 5s). So they are levels, not a total order.

The red ink draws directed edges along the arrangement graph, from vertices with smaller labels to larger ones. This is an acyclic orientation compatible with the level function: the order in which the sweep curve passes the vertices.

The two grids at the bottom right are wiring diagrams (Goodman's 'wiring diagram' / allowable-sequence encoding) of the same sweep.
- The first grid starts from the permutation A B C D E F G. Its levels 1–12 record the adjacent transpositions (crossings) met at each step.
- The second grid starts at level 12 with the intermediate permutation D F B E G C A. It continues through levels 12–19 and ends at the reversed order G F E D C B A.
- Together they describe the arrangement as a sequence of permutations from the identity to its reverse, each obtained by reversing adjacent blocks. This is a reduced decomposition of the longest element of S_7 when the arrangement is simple, and an allowable sequence in Goodman–Pollack's sense.

The margin notes ('9_1, 9_2, …') label simultaneous crossings at one level. The row '2 5 7 3 3 2' seems to count crossings, or the sizes of transposed blocks, in successive groups of levels. For seven lines in a simple arrangement there are C(7,2) = 21 crossings; the row sums to 22. Either the grouping overlaps at a shared level (for example level 12 counted in both halves) or the arrangement has a multiple point.

The previous page lists the same kind of permutation sequence (ABCDEFG → … → GAEDCFB, with primed levels 1'–9'). The next page shows more sweep sketches. So the purpose is to understand the dictionary between pseudo-line arrangements and sweeps / wiring diagrams / allowable sequences. In particular it checks that any arrangement can be swept by a pencil of pseudo-lines and read off as a sequence of adjacent transpositions.
errors: The row '2 5 7 3 3 2' sums to 22, but a simple arrangement of 7 pseudo-lines has 21 crossings. This suggests either a double count at the junction level 12 or a non-simple point. It is not clear from the image which.

The level labels are not all legible or consistent. Some vertices carry corrected or duplicated numbers (e.g. '14/15', '17/18', several 18s), so the drawn numbering may contain small bookkeeping slips. The page cannot settle this definitively.
The red arrows leaving at the right are labelled E, D, C. Whether these are boundary ends of the original lines or of an auxiliary red curve is ambiguous in the image.

ideas.what: Encoding a pseudo-line arrangement by sweeping it with a moving pseudo-line (here a pencil of curves through two poles) and recording the order of crossings by levels.
ideas.modern_name: Topological sweep / sweeping of pseudoline arrangements
ideas.usually_credited_to: Goodman–Pollack (early 1980s, allowable sequences); Edelsbrunner–Guibas (topological sweep, 1986/89); Snoeyink–Hershberger (sweeping arrangements of curves, 1989)

ideas.what: Wiring diagram: lines drawn as horizontal wires with crossings as local swaps, turning A..G into G..A, split across two half-sheets at level 12.
ideas.modern_name: Wiring diagram / allowable sequence of permutations / reduced word of the longest element w0 of S_n
ideas.usually_credited_to: J. E. Goodman (1980, wiring diagrams); Goodman–Pollack (allowable sequences)

ideas.what: Level function on vertices (several crossings at one level) inducing an acyclic orientation of the arrangement graph (red arrows).
ideas.modern_name: Linear extension / level structure of the sweep poset; orientation of the arrangement graph induced by a sweep

missed.claim: This is independent work by Grothendieck, around 1983–84, on the arrangement ↔ sweep ↔ wiring-diagram dictionary. It is contemporaneous with Goodman–Pollack and earlier than the Edelsbrunner–Guibas topological sweep. It is historically interesting as evidence of his combinatorial-geometric work after Esquisse, but the mathematics itself is standard.

missed.why_it_might_matter_today: This is of historical interest only. It documents Grothendieck's independent arrival at allowable sequences and sweeps, with no new mathematical content visible on this page.

deep.surprise_reason: This is a careful worked example of sweeping a 7-pseudo-line arrangement and reading off its wiring diagram. Those are well-known constructions credited to Goodman–Pollack and others. The page is of interest only as historical evidence of independent rediscovery.
transcription_corrections: The vertex labels 1–19 are sweep levels, not distinct vertices. Several vertices share a label (e.g. two 18s, two 19s, repeated 4 and 5).
The thin pencil curves between the top and bottom poles are a sweeping family (pencil). The transcription omits them.
The wiring diagrams carry marginal level annotations of the form '9_1, 9_2, …' for simultaneous crossings, which the transcription does not mention.
The first wiring diagram has a horizontal dashed sweep line around levels 3–4. The second has one near level 18.
